scenes.heading: On-Call & Runbooks
scenes.subheading: Being ready when the pager fires
scenes.narration: On-call is the practice of having someone ready to respond when a pipeline breaks, and runbooks are what keep that response calm and consistent.

scenes.heading: What good on-call looks like
bullets: A clear rotation so responsibility is never ambiguous
Escalation paths when the first responder is stuck
Humane load — sustainable shifts, not constant paging
Every page is actionable and worth waking up for
scenes.narration: A clear rotation ensures exactly one person knows they own the pager at any moment. Escalation paths give that person a defined way to pull in help when they are stuck. Shifts must stay humane so on-call does not burn people out. And every page should be actionable, because paging for something no one can act on only erodes trust.

scenes.heading: Anatomy of a runbook
scenes.narration: A runbook opens with the symptom and the exact alert that fired, so the responder knows they are in the right place. It states the impact and severity to guide urgency. Then it walks through diagnosis and concrete mitigation steps, and closes with who to escalate to if those steps fail.

scenes.heading: With vs without a runbook
scenes.narration: Without a runbook, incidents devolve into guesswork and quietly depend on the one engineer who happens to remember the fix. With a runbook, any on-call responder can follow calm, repeatable steps. The result is faster recovery that does not hinge on a single hero being awake.

scenes.text: Write the runbook while the incident is fresh, and link it directly from the alert so the fix is one click away at 3am.
scenes.narration: Write the runbook while the incident is still fresh in memory, and link it straight from the alert so the fix is one click away at three in the morning.
